newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden edges towards EMU 'no' - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Sweden edges towards EMU 'no' - analysts.

text.p: Sweden on Wednesday edged closer towards ending months of speculation and announce it would not join Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) at its 1999 start, analysts said.

A radio report said Prime Minister Goran Persson and Finance Minister Erik Asbrink had agreed the government could not join EMU during the current parliamentary term and that a general election would have to be held for Sweden to join EMU.

Analysts said this meant Swedish EMU membership would be delayed until after the next general election in 2002, unless the goverment held an extra election during the 1998-2002 mandate period. This is an uncommon practice in Sweden.
Market players said they interpreted this scenario as meaning Sweden could only join EMU after the 2002 elections.

Prime Minister Goran Persson would not comment on the report but a spokeswoman said that the ruling Social Democrats would announce their view shortly. Finance Minister Erik Asbrink called the report speculation.

A committee of the ruling Social Democratic Party formed to rule on Swedish adhesion to EMU will take its decision this Friday or on June 18, a party official said on Tuesday. A decision must be made before a party meeting on June 23.
Analysts were sceptical about Asbrink's comments.
"There's no smoke without fire. Of course there may be some truth in the report," Swedbank economist Ake Gustafsson told Reuters.
The next general election in Sweden is due to be held by September 1998.
"It's not entirely improbable that this is the way it is. If it's true it's a little more negative than what the financial markets had expected," Nordbanken economist Tomas Pousette said.
"Since they don't want to have a referendum the election in 2002 will be a natural opportunity to see if there is broad public support," Gustafsson said.
The debt market weakened slightly on the radio report but recovered slightly when the finance ministry dismissed the report as speculation, dealers said.
Future movement would hinge on news about EMU, with signs of a delayed Swedish membership having a negative effect.
However, most analysts seem to believe reaction on the debt market and by the currency would be limited and many said there was nothing new in the report.
"I don't believe there will be an enormous reaction on the market. There will be a bit of wait-and-see before the actual decision from the Social Democrats is announced," Pousette said.

"We have had a relatively strong market. This tendency can possibly break but I don't think the spread between longer Swedish and German bond yields will widen or that the crown will weaken sharply," Gustafsson said.
"There has been so much negative out about EMU lately that I don't think there will be any big effect," HSBC Midlands economist Peter Lindquist told Reuters.
"The only thing the report says is what the market already knows, that Sweden will not join EMU from its start in 1999 but will answer with a 'we'll wait and see' to the question," Lindquist said.
